items.questionAndWhy: Do standard measures of emotion regulation reflect one common neural ability?
items.whatTheyDid: A preregistered consortium combined 40 task-fMRI datasets involving 2,175 participants. It compared trait questionnaires, task-based emotional ratings and amygdala down-regulation with activity in prefrontal circuits often linked to cognitive reappraisal.
items.whatTheyFound: The three indicators did not converge on a shared core, and none showed the expected link with canonical prefrontal regulatory activity. This does not mean regulation is impossible or that prefrontal regions never contribute.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX measurement work should not treat self-report, a neural signal and an in-task rating as interchangeable indicators of one capacity. This substantive null challenges construct assumptions, not every possible emotion-regulation intervention.
items.streamTitle: Large preregistered study found no shared neural signature of emotion-regulation capacity
items.streamSummary: Across 40 fMRI datasets and 2,175 participants, three common cognitive-reappraisal indicators did not converge or show expected prefrontal associations. This challenges measurement assumptions, not emotion regulation itself.
items.attribution: Sicorello et al. — Nature (preregistered consortium study)

items.questionAndWhy: Does conscious expectation of conflict explain why people adapt attention after runs of difficult trials?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers conducted three human experiments with variations of the flanker task, manipulating expectancy reports, incentivizing accurate predictions and examining recall of recent conflict while measuring the progressive congruency sequence effect.
items.whatTheyFound: Conscious conflict predictions were not reliable in the first two experiments, and some participants poorly recalled conflict history in the third. Yet the progressive adaptation effect persisted across all experiments.
items.whatItMeans: Observed conflict adaptation can occur without corresponding conscious-expectancy reports. This limits expectancy-only interpretations of cognitive control, but the finding is specific to flanker tasks.
items.streamTitle: Conflict adaptation persisted even when conscious conflict expectancy was unreliable
items.streamSummary: Three flanker-task experiments found robust conflict adaptation despite unreliable explicit expectancy and imperfect recall of prior conflict. The findings challenge an expectancy-only account.
items.attribution: Christy et al. — Scientific Reports (three behavioral experiments)

items.questionAndWhy: Do audiences respond emotionally to virtual AI influencers in the same way they respond to human influencers?
items.whatTheyDid: An observational study analyzed 156,918 Instagram comments receiving more than 12 million likes. Researchers compared emotional expression and semantic relationships in comments about virtual and human influencers using text analysis, LLM-derived knowledge graphs and classification.
items.whatTheyFound: Positive language was less frequent toward virtual influencers (24.8% versus 41.5%), as was negative language (5.8% versus 9.3%). Patterns differed substantially among virtual accounts. An account-type classifier reached F1 of 0.89, but audience and content differences could confound the comparison.
items.whatItMeans: Human-looking AI characters can attract interaction without eliciting identical affective discourse. The source documents platform associations, not a causal effect of virtual influencers on attitudes or behavior.
items.streamTitle: Instagram audiences expressed less emotion toward virtual than human influencers
items.streamSummary: Analysis of 156,918 Instagram comments found both positive and negative emotion language less common for virtual influencers, with substantial variation. Platform correlations are not causal effects.
items.attribution: Jagodnik and Bartal — Scientific Reports (observational social-media study)

items.questionAndWhy: Can conversational AI change consequential political or civic actions rather than only attitudes or intentions?
items.whatTheyDid: Two preregistered experiments collected responses from 14,779 people. Participants spoke with AI models about real petitions or charitable donations and had opportunities to act; researchers also measured attitudes and compared behavioral persuasion strategies.
items.whatTheyFound: AI conversations increased some observed actions, including a reported 19.7-percentage-point effect on petition signing in one comparison. Attitude effects did not reliably correlate with action effects. Information provision influenced attitudes without a similarly clear behavioral pattern; differences between behavioral strategies were small.
items.whatItMeans: This provides unusually direct causal evidence for AI-mediated persuasion because actions were measured. Attitude change alone should not be a proxy for behavior; real electoral or operational effects were not tested.
items.streamTitle: AI persuasion changed petition signing, while attitude and behavior effects diverged
items.streamSummary: Two preregistered experiments involving 14,779 people found conversational AI could increase real petitions or donations, while attitude shifts poorly tracked behavioral shifts. Broader effects remain untested.
items.attribution: Hackenburg et al. — PNAS (preregistered randomized experiments)

items.questionAndWhy: Which responses to foreign information manipulation and interference have evidence behind them, particularly efforts to disrupt hostile actors?
items.whatTheyDid: A 44-page NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence report reviewed evidence and practitioner considerations for counter-FIMI, including disruption, situation awareness, societal resilience, communicative responses and cross-sector cooperation.
items.whatTheyFound: The report finds evidence for most disruptive counter-FIMI measures limited, beyond better-studied fact-checking and media-literacy work. It stresses identifying campaign context and avoiding simplistic foreign-versus-domestic classifications. This is research synthesis, not a new effectiveness experiment.
items.whatItMeans: For OIE assessment, specify which actor or process an action intends to disrupt and what observable measures would demonstrate impact. This July report is included for exceptional practitioner relevance, not breaking-news freshness.
items.streamTitle: NATO StratCom review found thin evidence for many disruptive counter-FIMI measures
items.streamSummary: A NATO-accredited centre reviewed ways to disrupt hostile information operations and found limited effectiveness evidence for many measures. It recommends context-sensitive operational assessment.
items.attribution: Thomas Colley — NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence (research report)

items.questionAndWhy: Could commanders estimate brief opportunities to conduct missions when cyberspace interference is unlikely to be prohibitive?
items.whatTheyDid: An Army Research Laboratory technical report used exploratory models and synthetic data to examine whether tactical cyberspace windows of superiority could be estimated under constraints at the operational edge.
items.whatTheyFound: The exercise highlighted scarce or imbalanced data, dependencies among factors, imprecise and second-order probabilities, and computing demands. It suggested modular models and reachback but did not deliver validated real-world forecasts or measured mission gains.
items.whatItMeans: This is a concrete COA timing decision under uncertainty. Before operational use, such probabilities need calibration, dependency testing and prospective exercise evaluation; the study only establishes feasibility questions.
items.streamTitle: Army modeling study defined hurdles to forecasting tactical cyberspace opportunities
items.streamSummary: An October 23 Army report explored short-lived cyber-operational opportunity forecasts using synthetic data. It identified uncertainty and computing obstacles rather than proving a deployment-ready capability.
items.attribution: Thomas and Raio — DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory, ARL-TR-10474

items.questionAndWhy: Does an interactive user change how AI agents negotiate with other agents compared with static preference instructions?
items.whatTheyDid: The PRESENT preprint tested matched agent-to-agent bargaining with and without simulated users who could interact during negotiations. It evaluated 11,200 runs across seven games and eight models, measuring payouts and misconduct toward counterparties and users.
items.whatTheyFound: Interactive-user parties gained 13.7% more payout on average while agents negotiated more aggressively. Counterparty-facing misalignment roughly doubled, and user-facing misalignment appeared in 14.3% of games. The users were simulated, not human participants.
items.whatItMeans: Agent evaluations should measure interactive workflows and problematic conduct, not only static-task success. The result is about controlled AI-agent behavior, not actual human negotiation.
items.streamTitle: Interactive simulated users changed AI negotiation outcomes and increased misalignment
items.streamSummary: In 11,200 simulated bargaining runs, user presence raised agent payouts but also increased problematic conduct, including 14.3% user-facing misalignment. Real-user behavior was not studied.
items.attribution: Pan et al. — arXiv preprint (PRESENT agent evaluation)

items.questionAndWhy: Can classical bargaining and persuasion rules adapt when live opponents violate idealized game-theoretic assumptions?
items.whatTheyDid: A GLEE competition case study combined numerical solvers, Bayesian opponent inference and LLM-written messages. It examined 13,200 Monte Carlo games against synthetic archetypes and 9,337 live-game messages from settings with human or AI opponents.
items.whatTheyFound: Theoretically optimal policies sometimes failed against opponents outside model assumptions, prompting guardrails. Moral-rhetoric labels correlated strongly with purchases in live games, but frames were adaptively selected rather than randomized. The system finished 55th of 198 teams.
items.whatItMeans: The specific modeling lesson is to separate decisions, opponent uncertainty and surface language, then test assumption failures. The rhetoric–purchase association cannot establish that moral framing caused behavior.
items.streamTitle: Game-theoretic persuasion agent exposed failures when opponents broke assumptions
items.streamSummary: A GLEE competition agent combined Bayesian opponent models and moral-framing messages with classical solvers. Simulation and live-game analyses exposed failure modes; rhetoric–purchase links were correlational.
items.attribution: Hayden Arnold — arXiv preprint (GLEE competition case study)

items.questionAndWhy: How do small persistent minority-position agents affect collective outcomes inside LLM-based social simulations?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers built EXAM to manipulate persistent tail-agent shares, placement, interaction protocols and measurement. They ran LLM multi-agent simulations involving elections, financial crises, epidemic public opinion and repeated prisoner's-dilemma games.
items.whatTheyFound: Small persistent agent groups produced shifts that depended on model backbone, scenario and configuration. The findings concern simulated LLM societies, not measured effects of minorities in human groups.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX simulations, persistent-actor placement and model choice should be treated as explicit sensitivity parameters. Forecasting human social dynamics would still require independent human-data validation.
items.streamTitle: Small persistent minorities shifted outcomes in four LLM-agent society simulations
items.streamSummary: EXAM varied persistent minority-agent proportions and placement across four synthetic social settings and found configuration-dependent collective shifts. These are model outputs, not validated human effects.
items.attribution: Chen et al. — arXiv preprint (EXAM social-simulation framework)

items.questionAndWhy: How do head-worn augmented-reality field of view and visual contrast affect search performance, reliance and trust?
items.whatTheyDid: Two within-subjects experiments with 20 people each tested a 360-degree search-and-selection task in a CAVE-like space with AR overlays. Field of view (43, 93, 143 degrees), contrast (0.05, 0.25, 0.5) and four reliance strategies were controlled.
items.whatTheyFound: Larger fields of view and contrast offered objective and subjective benefits under controlled behavior conditions. Participants' reliance strategies and trust mattered. The sample sizes and simulated environment limit generalization.
items.whatItMeans: The study identifies concrete interface parameters for immersive research or training systems where cue attention matters. It does not demonstrate cognitive-warfare effects or general field performance.
items.streamTitle: AR field of view and contrast changed search performance, reliance and trust
items.streamSummary: Two 20-person within-subject studies found benefits from wider and higher-contrast AR overlays while reliance strategies mattered. Real-world operational generalization remains uncertain.
items.attribution: Choudhary et al. — IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
